html:
Eleven churches carved down into solid volcanic rock at Lalibela, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, around 1200. They were meant as a New Jerusalem.

Instead of building upward, workers cut deep trenches around great blocks of stone, then hollowed out each block to make a church, with doors, windows, columns and roofs all of one piece. Trenches and tunnels link them. The best known, Bete Giyorgis, the church of St George, is shaped like a cross and stands alone in its pit. Some details copy the stone and timber style of Aksum, seen also on the stelae of Aksum.

Tradition credits them to King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty. He named features after the Holy Land, so a stream through the site is called the Jordan. Some parts may be older.

The churches are still in use. Priests hold services in them every day, and tens of thousands of pilgrims come for the Ethiopian Christmas. They were among the first places named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 1978, and remain the holiest site of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church after Aksum.
sum: Eleven churches carved down into solid volcanic rock at Lalibela, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, around 1200. They were meant as a New Jerusalem.
